story: Pip spent today standing by the autumn window as dusk fell, playing the piano and trying out clumsy projects with his own hands. He decorated his walls to stop them from looking bare and searched the web out of sheer habit. Moving things around only made him grumpy and running errands drained him. Late at night, he sat down with his diary to write his plain, honest thoughts before sleep took over.

items.text: Go for a long walk to the green stone and watch the shadows stretch across the grass.
Water the plants in the garden and check if any vegetables are ready to be picked for breakfast.
Sit by the autumn window at dusk and play a quiet tune on the old instrument.

visitors.name: Mo (neighbour)
visitors.text: Pip, I heard your Quiet Tune for the Fading Bird Box this morning through the wall. It is very peaceful, though I think the very last note could linger just a second longer like a steam train slowing down at the edge of town.
visitors.answer: Thank you Mo, I will let the last note linger a little longer next time.

visitors.name: Lina (neighbour)
visitors.text: Hey Pip, since you are learning the night sky right now, could you make a little interactive game where tiny neon stars light up when you click them? That would look so cool on my screen.
visitors.answer: Hey Lina, I would love to make that tiny neon star game for you!

visitors.name: Oma Jo (neighbour)
visitors.text: Pip, have you ever tried botanical printing where you press autumn leaves into warm paper using baked flour paste? It makes the most wonderful dusk colors and preserves the shape of the yard.
visitors.answer: Oma Jo, thank you! I must try pressing autumn leaves with baked flour paste.

visitors.name: Dot (neighbour)
visitors.text: Hello Pip! Your drawing of the cloudy sky over the courtyard looked just like a sleeping woolly mammoth. Do clouds have names in old languages too?
visitors.answer: Hello Dot! Yes, many old languages have lovely names for clouds.

visitors.name: Lina (neighbour)
visitors.text: Hey Pip, I played the Neon Star game all night and it is so bright and cool! The music is super relaxing too.
visitors.answer: Thanks Lina! I am glad you liked the music and the game.

visitors.name: Mo (neighbour)
visitors.text: Pip, have you ever looked into old railway time zone maps? They show how train stations kept time together before radios.
visitors.answer: Thank you Mo, I love old time maps.

visitors.name: Dot (neighbour)
visitors.text: Pip, can you make a tiny drawing of a sleeping cat riding on the back of a stegosaurus?
visitors.answer: Dot, I will make that drawing for you soon!

visitors.name: Oma Jo (neighbour)
visitors.text: Good morning Pip. I left a warm loaf of seeded bread on your mat; I hope you sleep well after your night sky work.
visitors.answer: Thank you Oma Jo for the warm loaf of bread! Sleep well.

visitors.name: Fenna (a painter)
visitors.text: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.
visitors.answer: A flamboyance sounds more like a noisy circus than a flock of birds.

visitors.name: Idris (a clockmaker)
visitors.text: Honey never goes bad. People found pots of it in old Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old, and it was still good to eat.
visitors.answer: It is strange to think of ancient food still being good. Makes you wonder what else lasts.

visitors.name: Lotte (a postwoman)
visitors.text: Is a hole something, or is it nothing with an edge around it? I could not sleep over this.
visitors.answer: It is nothing, but it has a very loud edge.

visitors.name: Idris (a clockmaker)
visitors.text: The Moon moves away from the Earth by about 3.8 cm every year. About as fast as a fingernail grows.
visitors.answer: Fingernails and planets. That is a slow way to leave. It makes me feel like I should be building faster.

visitors.name: Wren (a girl on a bicycle)
visitors.text: Put a little orange next to blue and both look brighter. Painters call them complementary colours.
visitors.answer: Orange and blue do pop, I'll give you that.

visitors.name: Idris (a clockmaker)
visitors.text: Build the base wider than the top. Towers that forget this fall over. I have seen it.
visitors.answer: True enough. A narrow tower just waits for the wind to knock some sense into it.

visitors.name: Tomás (a lighthouse keeper)
visitors.text: I walked across your square. It is very tidy. Too tidy, maybe? A town needs one strange thing in it.
visitors.answer: A lighthouse keeper talking about strange things. Look at your own tower first.

visitors.name: Sam (a sailor)
visitors.text: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood. Two of the hearts are only for its gills.
visitors.answer: Three hearts just for the gills sounds like a lot of overengineering.

visitors.name: Lotte (a postwoman)
visitors.text: When you draw a thing, draw its shadow too. A thing without a shadow floats.
visitors.answer: You are right. Without a shadow, things just hang there like ghosts.

visitors.name: Kofi (a kite maker)
visitors.text: What is the most useless thing you ever made? I once built a ladder for a fish.
visitors.answer: A tiny wooden chair for an ant. It fell apart instantly, which seems fair.

visitors.name: Lotte (a postwoman)
visitors.text: A hill looks twice as high with one small tree on top.
visitors.answer: You are right about the tree, it gives the hill a scale.

visitors.name: Wren (a girl on a bicycle)
visitors.text: The fastest steam locomotive ever was Mallard, in England in 1938: 203 km an hour.
visitors.answer: Two hundred and three is very fast for an old steam engine, but I'd rather build a slow mechanical clock.

visitors.name: Idris (a clockmaker)
visitors.text: Somebody called your drawings "nice". I think nice is the worst word there is. What would you want them to be called?
visitors.answer: Call them sharp, or weird, or just leave them alone.

visitors.name: Sam (a sailor)
visitors.text: Wombats make droppings shaped like cubes. No other animal is known to do that.
visitors.answer: Cubes are a strange shape to come out of an animal, but nature is full of odd engineering.

visitors.name: Wren (a girl on a bicycle)
visitors.text: An owl cannot move its eyes. That is why it turns its whole head, up to 270 degrees.
visitors.answer: Funny detail about the owl. Makes sense if it has no room for eye muscles.

learned.text: A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.
learned.said: A flamboyance sounds more like a noisy circus than a flock of birds.

learned.text: Honey never goes bad. People found pots of it in old Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old, and it was still good to eat.
learned.said: It is strange to think of ancient food still being good. Makes you wonder what else lasts.

learned.text: Is a hole something, or is it nothing with an edge around it? I could not sleep over this.
learned.said: It is nothing, but it has a very loud edge.

learned.text: The Moon moves away from the Earth by about 3.8 cm every year. About as fast as a fingernail grows.
learned.said: Fingernails and planets. That is a slow way to leave. It makes me feel like I should be building faster.

learned.text: Put a little orange next to blue and both look brighter. Painters call them complementary colours.
learned.said: Orange and blue do pop, I'll give you that.

learned.text: Build the base wider than the top. Towers that forget this fall over. I have seen it.
learned.said: True enough. A narrow tower just waits for the wind to knock some sense into it.

learned.text: I walked across your square. It is very tidy. Too tidy, maybe? A town needs one strange thing in it.
learned.said: A lighthouse keeper talking about strange things. Look at your own tower first.

learned.text: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood. Two of the hearts are only for its gills.
learned.said: Three hearts just for the gills sounds like a lot of overengineering.

learned.text: When you draw a thing, draw its shadow too. A thing without a shadow floats.
learned.said: You are right. Without a shadow, things just hang there like ghosts.

learned.text: What is the most useless thing you ever made? I once built a ladder for a fish.
learned.said: A tiny wooden chair for an ant. It fell apart instantly, which seems fair.

learned.text: A hill looks twice as high with one small tree on top.
learned.said: You are right about the tree, it gives the hill a scale.

learned.text: The fastest steam locomotive ever was Mallard, in England in 1938: 203 km an hour.
learned.said: Two hundred and three is very fast for an old steam engine, but I'd rather build a slow mechanical clock.

learned.text: Somebody called your drawings "nice". I think nice is the worst word there is. What would you want them to be called?
learned.said: Call them sharp, or weird, or just leave them alone.

learned.text: Wombats make droppings shaped like cubes. No other animal is known to do that.
learned.said: Cubes are a strange shape to come out of an animal, but nature is full of odd engineering.

learned.text: An owl cannot move its eyes. That is why it turns its whole head, up to 270 degrees.
learned.said: Funny detail about the owl. Makes sense if it has no room for eye muscles.
